source.title: Start with the person and the purpose
source.deliverable: Choose a work example and describe the intended experience

sections.title: Welcome to your learning
paragraphs: Welcome. This learning is about making the work you already do more understandable, accessible and responsive to people. You do not need to know every culture or have authority over an entire program to begin. You do need a willingness to notice, ask, and follow through.

Across these lessons, we will use the National CLAS Standards to examine practical decisions. The name refers to culturally and linguistically appropriate services. The standards come from the United States Department of Health and Human Services Office of Minority Health. They provide a framework for organizations. Here, we will connect that framework to individual work within the Disability Services Division.

This is voluntary, self-directed learning. You can pause, revisit an explanation, or take a break. You do not need a partner or a group. When you reach a reflection, you can think quietly, use your own notes, or work with the companion sheet. You do not need to share personal experiences. Please leave names, case details, health information and other private information out of your learning notes.

sections.title: Choose something you can work with
paragraphs: Choose one ordinary part of your work that you can examine safely. It might be a public notice, an instruction, a form, a meeting invitation, an internal process, or a recommendation you help prepare. If you do not have an example in mind, follow the sample service notice that we will use throughout this curriculum.

Our sample notice asks a person to attend a service-planning conversation. It explains the date but uses unfamiliar acronyms. It provides a telephone number without explaining how to request communication assistance. Staff have noticed that some people do not respond. Those observations give us questions to explore. They do not tell us why any particular person did not respond.

For your own example, write one sentence about its purpose. Then describe what the person receiving it needs to be able to do. Those are different questions. The organization's purpose may be to schedule a meeting. The person's task may be to understand why the meeting matters, consider their choices, arrange the support they want, and respond in a way they can use.
Pause here if you would like to choose your example. You can change it later.

sections.title: The principal standard
paragraphs: Standard one is the foundation. In practical terms, it asks us to provide quality services that people can understand, that respect them, and that respond to their cultural beliefs, language, health literacy and other communication needs. This explanation is a guide to application. The original wording is available beside the lesson.

Notice that the focus is the person's experience of the service, not simply whether we sent information. A letter can be accurate and still be difficult to use. An interpreter can be scheduled and still arrive too late for meaningful participation. A form can be online and still be inaccessible to someone who uses assistive technology or does not have reliable internet access.

Equity asks us to consider what people need to participate meaningfully. Giving everyone the same format does not tell us whether everyone can use it. At the same time, we should not assume a person's needs from their name, appearance, disability, language or community membership. Ask respectfully, offer choices within the available process, and confirm whether the response works.

sections.title: How the standards connect
paragraphs: There are fifteen standards. Standard one states the central purpose. Standards two through four address governance, leadership and workforce. Standards five through eight address communication and language assistance. Standards nine through fifteen address engagement, improvement and accountability.

These are connected responsibilities. A staff member may recognize that a notice needs a clear offer of language assistance. Making that offer dependable may also require an approved process, trained staff, resources, community input and a way to monitor whether assistance actually reaches people. That is why we will move between everyday interactions and the organizational conditions that support them.

You are not expected to personally perform every organizational responsibility. Part of good practice is recognizing the difference between a change within your authority and an issue that needs coordination or approval. We will return to that distinction throughout the curriculum.

sections.title: Try a first decision
paragraphs: Consider the sample notice. The team wants to improve response rates. One suggestion is to send the same notice more often. Another is to ask how people experience the notice and examine whether its instructions and assistance options are usable. Which approach gives you a better starting point for understanding the barrier?
Pause and make your choice in the activity below. The feedback will explain the reasoning. You can revise your answer; the purpose is to practice.

Sending a reminder may eventually help, but repeating an unclear message can repeat the same barrier. Start by understanding the experience. That does not mean delaying every action until you have perfect information. It means making a reasonable inquiry, trying an appropriate change, and checking what happened.

sections.title: Your first working note
paragraphs: Finish this lesson with three short notes: the work example you chose, the person or people who need to use it, and what successful participation would look like from their perspective. Keep these notes general and free of personal information.

In the next lesson, we will look more closely at the difference between an observation and an assumption. That distinction helps us ask better questions and choose a useful response. For now, remember this starting point: a process is not fully understood by looking only at what we send or what we intend. We also need to learn how people encounter and use it.

practice.question: Several people have not responded to a service-planning notice. What is the most useful first step?

options.text: Send the same notice more often before examining the process.
options.feedback: A reminder may help some people, but repeating the same message can repeat the same barrier. First examine how people receive, understand and use the notice.

options.text: Examine the notice and response routes, and seek appropriate information about people's experience.
options.feedback: This begins with inquiry. Check the purpose, next step, assistance offer and available feedback without assuming why any individual has not responded.

options.text: Conclude that people who do not respond are not interested.
options.feedback: A response pattern does not establish motivation. Language, format, timing, delivery and other conditions may affect participation.

practice.reflection: Choose one non-sensitive work example. What is its purpose, who needs to use it, and what would successful participation look like?

example.title: Our working example: a service-planning notice
example.situation: A notice gives a meeting date, uses several unfamiliar terms and lists a telephone number without explaining how to request communication assistance. Some recipients do not respond.
example.response: Begin by describing the person's task: understand why the meeting matters, consider their choices, arrange the support they want and use a clear response route.
example.reason: This separates the organization's task of sending a notice from the person's experience of using it.

source.title: Notice barriers and ask without assumptions
source.deliverable: Separate an observation from an assumption; write a respectful question

sections.title: Begin with what you know
paragraphs: In the first lesson, you chose a work example and described what someone needs to do with it. Now we will examine what might get in the way. This lesson connects the principal standard with ongoing workforce learning and understanding community needs.

Start with an observation you could describe without assigning a motive. For our sample notice, the observation is that some people have not responded. Saying that they do not care is an interpretation. Saying that they cannot understand the notice is also an interpretation until we have more information.

A respectful inquiry begins by acknowledging what we do not know. We can say, where our role permits contact, that we want to check whether the person received the information and whether another way of explaining or responding would help. We do not need to begin by asking the person to defend their behavior.

sections.title: Look at the whole encounter
paragraphs: Imagine the steps involved in responding. The person must receive the notice, recognize its purpose, understand the options, decide what they want to do, and use an available response method. A difficulty at any one step can look like a lack of interest from the other end.

Possible barriers include unfamiliar terminology, information in a format someone cannot access, no interpreter when needed, an inconvenient appointment, transportation, unreliable technology, or previous experiences that make the process difficult to trust. These are possibilities to investigate, not explanations to assign automatically.

Also look for strengths and supports. A person may already have an effective communication method, a trusted support person they choose, or a clear preference about how to receive information. A community may have organizations with relevant knowledge and established relationships. Understanding assets as well as barriers is part of the community assessment described in standard twelve.

sections.title: Culture is a starting point for curiosity
paragraphs: Culture can shape communication, expectations and experiences. It does not determine every person's preferences. People within the same community differ, and a person's preferences can change with the situation.

Avoid turning general information about a community into a rule about an individual. Instead of deciding that a family will want a particular person to speak, ask whom the person would like involved and how they want to participate. Instead of interpreting silence as agreement, offer time and a way to ask questions. Instead of treating an accent as evidence of understanding or misunderstanding, check the clarity of the information itself.

Cultural humility involves examining your own assumptions as well. Familiar procedures can feel straightforward to the people who use them every day. They may be entirely unfamiliar to someone encountering them for the first time. Recognizing that difference is an opportunity to improve the explanation.

sections.title: Practice a useful question
paragraphs: Consider these two openings. The first asks, why have you failed to return the form? The second explains the purpose of the form, asks whether the person received it, and offers help identifying a usable way to respond. The second opening provides information and creates room for the person's explanation.

That does not mean ignoring a deadline or a required step. It means explaining the requirement clearly while asking what support is needed. Do not promise an extension or exception that you cannot authorize. If an adjustment needs approval, explain what you can do next and who will review it.

In the practice activity, separate what was observed from what was assumed. Then choose a question that invites the person's perspective without requiring private information that is not needed for the task.

sections.title: Apply inquiry to your own role
paragraphs: You may not have direct contact with people receiving services. If you work on policy, data, contracts or communications, inquiry still matters. Ask how the process was tested, whose experience informed it, which access needs were considered, and where feedback is recorded. Consult the appropriate people rather than inventing an answer or contacting someone outside your responsibilities.

A supervisor can help staff discuss uncertainty without shaming them for asking questions. A manager can look for repeated barriers across encounters. A director can ask whether resources and accountability support the response. Regular learning, addressed in standard four, should help people practice these decisions rather than merely acknowledge that they read a policy.

sections.title: Add to your working example
paragraphs: Return to your selected work example. Write one observation, one assumption you need to set aside, and one respectful question that would help you learn more. Then identify an appropriate way to obtain that information within your role.

If there is no direct access to the people affected, do not fill the gap by guessing. Name the gap and identify who can help. Existing feedback, approved engagement processes, accessibility reviews or a discussion with the responsible program area may provide a starting point.

The next lesson follows a language-assistance request through an encounter. Keep the habit from this lesson with you: ask about needs and preferences, describe what you know, and leave room for information that could change your first interpretation.

practice.question: A person has missed two appointments. Which note best separates observation from assumption?

options.text: They missed two appointments, so they do not value the service.
options.feedback: The first part is an observation; the conclusion assigns a motive without evidence.

options.text: They missed two appointments because people from their community prefer another process.
options.feedback: A generalization about a community does not explain this person's experience. Ask rather than assign a cultural explanation.

options.text: Two appointments were missed. We need to learn whether the information, timing, communication or another part of the process was difficult to use.
options.feedback: This describes what is known and identifies questions. Use the appropriate contact or review process to learn more, without collecting unnecessary private information.

practice.reflection: Write one observation, one assumption to set aside and one respectful question. How could you obtain the answer within your role?

example.title: Replace a conclusion with a question
example.situation: A colleague says, 'People who do not reply are not interested.' The available information only shows that a reply was not received.
example.response: Ask what is known about delivery, understanding, timing and available response methods. Where contact is appropriate, ask whether the person received the notice and whether another explanation or response method would help.
example.reason: The question leaves room for the person's explanation and avoids treating an assumption as evidence.

source.title: Make language assistance usable
source.deliverable: Trace an assistance request from offer through follow-up

sections.title: Follow the request through
paragraphs: Language assistance is useful when someone can find it, request it and receive it in time to participate. In this lesson, we will connect standards five, six and seven to the steps before, during and after an encounter.

Standard five addresses timely language assistance without cost to the individual. Standard six addresses making people aware of that assistance orally and in writing. Standard seven addresses the competence of people providing language assistance. The standards work together: an available service does little good if someone does not know about it or cannot request it.

For your specific work, use current agency procedures and the responsible program's guidance. This lesson does not establish a new vendor, reimbursement rule, eligibility rule or approval process. Knowing how to locate the right procedure is part of being prepared.

sections.title: Before the encounter
paragraphs: Return to the service-planning notice. It gives a date and a number to call, but does not explain how to request assistance. A practical review asks whether the notice makes assistance visible, whether the request method is usable, and whether someone is responsible for responding.

Ask about preferred language and communication needs respectfully, using an approved process. Do not assume that a person wants an interpreter because of their name or accent, or assume that they do not because they can hold a brief conversation in English. Understanding everyday conversation and understanding a complex service decision are different tasks.

When an interpreter is needed, follow the applicable arrangements early enough to support participation. Confirm the language, any relevant communication needs, the setting, timing and the information required for the assignment. Share only information that is appropriate and necessary through the approved channels. A request is not complete merely because it was sent; someone needs to confirm the arrangement and know what to do if it fails.

sections.title: Support people and interpreter roles
paragraphs: Consider a person who arrives with a family member and says that the family member has been helping with communication. Treat both people respectfully. Do not assume that the family member is qualified to interpret complex information, and do not confuse the person's chosen support with the organization's responsibility to provide appropriate communication assistance.

The CLAS framework discourages using untrained individuals and minors as interpreters. Applicable laws and agency procedures also matter. Follow those requirements and seek the appropriate guidance rather than making a blanket decision based only on this example. Explain the available assistance, ask about the person's preferences, and preserve their involvement in decisions.

A qualified interpreter and a chosen support person can have different roles. One conveys communication accurately; the other may provide the support the person wants. Clarifying roles helps avoid putting someone in a position they are not prepared or authorized to fill.

sections.title: During the encounter
paragraphs: Address the person directly. Use clear language and manageable portions of information. Allow time for interpretation and questions. Avoid speaking about the person as though they are not present. Check whether the communication method is working, and respond if there is a problem.

Checking understanding should not feel like testing or blaming the person. You can explain that you want to check whether your explanation of the next step was clear, then invite them to explain what they understand will happen. If the explanation was unclear, try again in a different way. Do not simply repeat the same wording more loudly.

If assistance is unavailable or unsuitable, follow the approved contingency and escalation process. Do not improvise with a child, an unapproved automated tool, or an unqualified bystander to complete a consequential conversation. Explain what you can do now and how the communication need will be addressed. Urgent circumstances require the applicable urgent-response procedure, not a rule invented by this lesson.

sections.title: After the encounter
paragraphs: Confirm the next step in a form the person can use. Record operational information required by the applicable procedure, using approved systems and appropriate privacy protections. A learning worksheet is not a case record.

If there was a delay or repeated difficulty arranging assistance, raise that pattern through the appropriate channel. Individual staff should not have to solve the same preventable problem repeatedly without organizational support. That connection will matter when we discuss leadership, resources and improvement.

sections.title: Practice and carry it forward
paragraphs: In the activity below, decide which next step best supports a person whose assistance request has not been confirmed. Look for an answer that checks the arrangement, communicates with the person and uses the appropriate escalation route. An answer that simply assumes someone else handled it leaves the barrier unresolved.

For your work example, identify where assistance is offered, how it is requested, who responds and how completion is confirmed. If you do not know one of those steps, record a question for the responsible area. Do not enter anyone's personal details.

You now have a way to examine the whole request, rather than just the presence of an assistance statement. Next, we will look at the information itself: whether someone can find the message, access it, understand it, use it and act on it.

practice.question: An assistance request was sent, but no one has confirmed the arrangement for a planned conversation. What should happen next?

options.text: Check the arrangement through the approved process, communicate with the person and use the appropriate escalation route if needed.
options.feedback: A sent request is not a confirmed arrangement. Follow the applicable procedure and make sure the person knows what will happen. Do not promise a service or change outside your authority.

options.text: Assume the request was handled because it was sent to the usual address.
options.feedback: That leaves the communication need unconfirmed. Someone needs responsibility for follow-through and a contingency if the arrangement fails.

options.text: Plan to ask any available family member to interpret if assistance is unavailable.
options.feedback: A support person's role is not automatically an interpreter's role. Follow the applicable requirements for appropriate assistance rather than improvising with an unqualified person.

practice.reflection: For your example, where is assistance offered, how is it requested, who responds and how is completion confirmed? Note gaps as questions, not guessed procedures.

example.title: A request needs follow-through
example.situation: An assistance request has been forwarded, but the arrangement has not been confirmed before the planned conversation.
example.response: The responsible staff member checks the request through the approved route, confirms the arrangement or escalates the gap, and communicates the next step to the person in a usable way.
example.reason: Availability, awareness and competent assistance need to work together. Sending a request does not establish that assistance will be provided.

source.title: Make information accessible and actionable
source.deliverable: Review and improve a notice or process instruction

sections.title: Examine the information itself
paragraphs: You have considered the person's experience and the path for communication assistance. Now take a closer look at the information. Standard eight addresses understandable digital and print materials and signage in languages used by people served. The principal standard keeps the person's communication needs at the center.

We will use five questions: can the person find it, access it, understand it, use it and act on it? These questions are a practical review aid. They do not replace technical accessibility testing, translation review or applicable agency requirements. They help you recognize where further work is needed.

Choose a public-facing or non-sensitive example for this activity. If you are reviewing a real work document, keep it in the appropriate work location rather than placing personal information in your learning notes.

sections.title: Find and access
paragraphs: First, can the person find the information? A statement about assistance may exist somewhere on a website but be absent from the notice where the person needs it. A link may use an internal document name that gives no clue about its purpose. A telephone option may be difficult to locate among several unrelated numbers.

Next, can the person access it? Consider format and method, not only whether the file opens on your computer. An image of text may be unreadable to assistive technology. A video without accurate captions or a useful transcript may exclude people. A form that requires a mouse can block keyboard users. A digital-only instruction may be unusable without reliable access to a suitable device or connection.

Do not assume you can determine every accessibility issue by looking at the screen. Use the established review process and involve the appropriate accessibility support. If you create documents, use meaningful headings, descriptive links, readable structure and the approved tools for checking the result. Check the document that people will actually receive, including any exported version.

sections.title: Understand the message
paragraphs: Look at our sample notice. It asks the person to attend a service-planning meeting, but the opening sentence is filled with acronyms and internal references. The reader may not know what the meeting is for, whether they have a choice, or what they need to do next.

A clearer structure begins with purpose and action. Explain why the person is receiving the notice. Identify the next step, the relevant date and a way to ask questions or request assistance. Explain necessary terms when they first appear. Keep essential rights, choices and requirements intact; plain language is not permission to remove important meaning.

Translation and plain language solve related but different problems. A translated document can still be difficult to understand if the source is unnecessarily complicated. An easy-to-read English version does not meet every language need. Use the appropriate qualified review and approved process for the actual audience and purpose. Do not send confidential information into an unapproved translation service.

sections.title: Use and act
paragraphs: Now ask whether the person can use the information to make a decision or complete a step. A notice might say to contact the department without naming a usable route. A form might explain what is needed but provide no way to ask for help. A deadline might be stated without explaining what action must be completed by that date.

Make the next step concrete. In our learning example, a useful notice would explain the meeting's purpose, how to confirm or discuss the appointment, how to request communication assistance, and where to ask questions. Use actual approved contact details in real work. We are not inventing a new contact or process here.

Check that the proposed change is within your authority. You may be able to improve a draft, but a regulated notice or official form may require review before use. Preserve the required content and route the suggested revision to the person responsible.

sections.title: Try a communication review
paragraphs: In the activity, compare three proposed revisions to the notice. Think about what each option would mean for someone who needs to understand the information and act on it. Consider clarity, accessibility, required meaning and a way to request assistance. Choose the strongest revision, then read the feedback.

Then apply the five questions to your example. You do not have to solve every issue today. Identify one change you can propose or make, one item that needs specialist review, and one way to check whether the revised information is more usable.

Where appropriate, feedback from people who use the information can reveal issues that an internal review misses. That feedback should be accessible and voluntary, with a clear explanation of how it will be used. We will develop that approach in the community-partnership lesson.

sections.title: Carry the change forward
paragraphs: Save a short description of the improvement in your own notes: the barrier, the proposed change, the necessary review and the expected benefit. Avoid claiming that a document is fully accessible simply because it passed one automated check or received a positive comment.
The goal is a more dependable experience. In the next lesson, we will connect your proposed improvement to the roles, resources and decisions that make it possible to sustain.

practice.question: Which proposed notice revision is strongest?

options.text: Remove technical terms and all required details so the notice is shorter.
options.feedback: Shorter is not necessarily clearer or complete. Preserve essential rights, choices and requirements, and obtain the required review.

options.text: Explain the purpose, next step and assistance route in clear language while preserving required meaning and checking accessibility.
options.feedback: This addresses understanding and action together. Translation, accessibility and official-content review may still be needed; one check is not enough.

options.text: Keep the wording and publish it as a picture so its layout stays consistent.
options.feedback: An image of text may be inaccessible to assistive technology and does not address unclear wording. Use an accessible format and the appropriate checks.

practice.reflection: Can someone find, access, understand, use and act on your example? Identify one change, one specialist-review need and one way to check usability.

example.title: Compare the structure of a notice
example.situation: Less useful: 'Please attend your annual review. Contact our office if needed.' The purpose, response task and assistance route are unclear.
example.response: Clearer structure: explain why the conversation is happening; state the date and response step; explain how to discuss an alternative arrangement or ask questions; include the approved language and disability assistance information. Use actual authorized wording and contact details in the real notice.
example.reason: This is a learning example, not an official notice. The revision must preserve required information and receive the applicable review before use.

source.title: Connect your role with organizational responsibility
source.deliverable: Identify what you can change, who must approve and what support is needed

sections.title: Individual action needs support
paragraphs: So far, you have identified a work example, asked about barriers, traced assistance and considered the information itself. Some improvements may be within your control. Others depend on authority, resources or coordination. Recognizing that distinction is part of effective practice.

Standards two, three and four address governance, leadership and workforce. Standard nine connects goals, policies and accountability to operations. Together, they remind us that culturally and linguistically appropriate services cannot depend only on one person's effort or goodwill.

In this lesson, choose the perspective closest to your responsibilities. You can also explore the others. The examples describe possible contributions, not a new assignment of duties. Use your actual role, current procedures and supervisory guidance to determine what you can decide.

sections.title: If your contribution is an everyday task
paragraphs: You might prepare information, answer questions, support a meeting, review a document, analyze a process or identify a recurring problem. Your contribution can begin with careful observation, a respectful question, a well-supported suggestion and follow-through on the work you own.

For the sample notice, you may be able to identify unclear instructions and propose a revision. You may not be authorized to change a required deadline or replace an approved notice. A useful next step is to describe the barrier, preserve the required meaning and send the proposed improvement to the person responsible.

Avoid carrying an unresolved access problem privately from one encounter to the next. Use the appropriate route to identify repeated difficulties, while protecting personal information. Raising a pattern with clear evidence gives others something they can act on.

sections.title: If you supervise people
paragraphs: A supervisor can help staff prepare for access needs, locate procedures and practice difficult conversations. Coaching can begin with questions: what did you observe, what did you ask, what remains uncertain, and what support do you need?

Discuss the work without reducing the person receiving services to a label. Help staff distinguish an access barrier from an assumption about motivation. Make room for questions and appropriate escalation. A person who identifies a gap should not have to pretend they already know how to resolve it.

Standard four addresses regular education and training. A useful learning opportunity connects to the work staff do and the choices they face. A brief review of a notice or an assistance request can be more useful than repeating a definition without practicing its use.

sections.title: If you manage a process or resources
paragraphs: A manager may be able to examine recurring patterns, clarify ownership, allocate available resources and coordinate changes. For our notice, that could mean identifying who maintains the text, who arranges assistance, how requests are tracked and how problems are reviewed.

Ask whether the proposed process is dependable when the usual contact is unavailable. Consider workload and capacity. An instruction to offer assistance is incomplete if staff have no workable way to arrange it. An improvement plan needs an owner, appropriate resources and a way to evaluate whether it works.

Do not interpret a difference in participation as proof of one cause. Use it as a reason to investigate. The evidence lesson will show how to combine operational information with experience and context.

sections.title: If you set direction or advise leadership
paragraphs: Leadership responsibilities include making expectations visible in policy, planning, resources and accountability. Standard two addresses sustained organizational support. Standard three addresses a workforce and leadership equipped to respond to the needs of the population.

This should not become an assumption that one employee represents an entire community or should provide informal interpreting because of their identity. Capability, preparation, appropriate role assignments and support matter. Recruitment, development and promotion practices should follow applicable requirements while considering the skills and experience needed to serve people effectively.

Someone advising leadership can frame a decision clearly: here is the access problem, here is the evidence and uncertainty, here are the options, and here is what each option requires. The recommendation should explain who will be affected and how their perspectives will inform the decision.

sections.title: Map the next step
paragraphs: For your work example, separate three categories. First, what can you change within your responsibilities? Second, what requires coordination or review? Third, what needs a decision by someone with different authority?

For each proposed action, identify the responsible role rather than inventing a person's name. Add the resource or information needed and a reasonable next step. If ownership is unclear, clarifying ownership can itself be the next action.

In the practice activity, choose the response that advances the improvement without exceeding authority or abandoning the concern. Neither changing an official requirement on your own nor leaving the problem unraised is a complete response.

sections.title: Connect responsibility with participation
paragraphs: Your role map makes the improvement more realistic. It also reveals who has not yet been heard. In the next lesson, we will consider how the people affected can inform a change before the decision is already made.

practice.question: You identify a barrier in an official notice but do not have authority to change the requirement. What is a useful response?

options.text: Change the requirement yourself because the goal is important.
options.feedback: An important goal does not expand your authority. Preserve the requirement and route a supported proposal to the person responsible.

options.text: Leave the issue unraised because you cannot approve the change.
options.feedback: You can still document the barrier and recommend a next step. Raising a well-described problem is a meaningful contribution.

options.text: Describe the barrier, propose a revision that preserves the required meaning and identify the right person.
options.feedback: This advances the work responsibly. Clarify ownership, resources and the next review step rather than assuming approval.

practice.reflection: What can you change directly? What needs coordination? What requires another person's decision? Identify roles, resources and a next step.

example.title: Turn a concern into a supported proposal
example.situation: You can identify unclear wording but cannot approve a change to the official notice.
example.response: Prepare a concise description of the barrier, a suggested revision that preserves the requirement, the relevant access questions and a request for review by the responsible role.
example.reason: A specific proposal moves the work forward without changing requirements outside your authority.

source.title: Learn with people affected by the work
source.deliverable: Plan meaningful, accessible input and explain how it will influence a decision

sections.title: Ask before the decision is settled
paragraphs: Imagine a team revises the service-planning notice and asks for feedback only after the new version is approved and distributed. People may offer useful observations, but they have little opportunity to influence the original decision. Participation has arrived too late.

Standards twelve and thirteen address understanding community assets and needs and partnering with communities in the design, implementation and evaluation of practice. For your individual work, the question is how you can support an appropriate process for learning with people affected, within your responsibilities.

This lesson does not require you to organize a group or personally contact service recipients. You can complete every activity independently. Where engagement is needed, identify the established route and the people responsible for it.

sections.title: Clarify what can change
paragraphs: Before asking for input, describe the decision. What is open to change? What requirements or constraints must remain? How will input be considered, who will decide, and when will people hear what happened?

For the notice, the team may be able to change the wording, layout and explanation of assistance, while a required time limit remains fixed. Say that clearly. Asking people to choose something that is not actually open can damage trust. A constrained decision can still benefit from meaningful participation when the boundaries are honest.

Also ask whose experience is missing. People who readily respond to an online survey may not represent those who had difficulty accessing the original information. A single community member cannot be assumed to speak for every person with a disability, every language community or every family.

sections.title: Make participation usable
paragraphs: Consider the format, language, communication support, timing, location or technology, and the effort required. An invitation that is inaccessible can reproduce the very problem the project hopes to address. Offer appropriate ways to participate through the approved engagement process.

Respect a person's choice not to participate. Avoid making access to services appear dependent on providing feedback. Explain what information is requested, how it will be used and any limits on confidentiality. Follow applicable privacy and records requirements. If compensation or reimbursement is available, use the established rules; do not promise a payment you cannot authorize.

Participation should make room for the person themselves, including self-advocates and their chosen supports. Do not automatically substitute the views of professionals or family members for the person's perspective. At the same time, different perspectives can reveal different parts of an experience when their roles are clear.

sections.title: Listen for assets as well as problems
paragraphs: Community assessment includes strengths. Ask what already works, which communication approaches are trusted, and what people would want preserved. A redesign can unintentionally remove a feature that some people depend on.

In our example, a clear telephone option may be valuable even if a new online response form is introduced. Improving one route does not necessarily justify removing another. Look for choices that support participation rather than assuming one channel will work for everyone.

When feedback differs, describe the difference rather than forcing agreement. One person may prefer a brief notice, while another needs more explanation. A concise main message with accessible supporting detail might address both needs, but the proposed solution still needs checking.

sections.title: Close the loop
paragraphs: After input is considered, explain what changed, what did not change and why. Be specific without exposing personal information. If a suggestion cannot be adopted, acknowledge it and explain the relevant constraint or next step. Silence can leave people unsure whether their contribution mattered.

Partnership continues into implementation and evaluation. People can help identify whether the revised notice actually improves understanding or whether a new barrier has appeared. That is different from using a consultation only to endorse a finished product.

sections.title: Plan your contribution
paragraphs: For your work example, write the decision that needs input, the perspectives that may be missing, an accessible way to obtain that input, and the role responsible for arranging it. Then describe how people would hear back.

If you lack authority to initiate engagement, your action might be a recommendation to the responsible person. It can still be precise: ask for input before approval, identify the access considerations, and explain how the input could improve the decision.

In the practice activity, choose an approach that gives people a real opportunity to influence the work while being honest about constraints. The aim is not simply to count participants. It is to improve the decision and the experience through meaningful involvement.
Next, we will consider how to tell whether the change is helping. Your plan for participation will be part of that evidence.

practice.question: A team wants input on a notice. Which approach offers the most meaningful participation?

options.text: Seek accessible input before approval, explain what can change and report back on how the input affected the decision.
options.feedback: This gives input a genuine purpose and closes the loop. Use the established engagement process and be honest about constraints.

options.text: Ask for endorsement after the finished notice is distributed.
options.feedback: People have little opportunity to shape a decision that is already complete. Later evaluation can help, but it does not replace earlier participation.

options.text: Ask one person to represent everyone who may receive the notice.
options.feedback: One perspective can be valuable without representing every experience. Identify whose perspectives are missing and appropriate ways to include them.

practice.reflection: What decision needs input? Whose perspective is missing? Who can arrange accessible participation, and how will people hear what happened?

example.title: Invite input while it can matter
example.situation: The team intends to ask people whether they like a revised notice after it is approved.
example.response: Recommend an accessible review before approval. Explain what can change, seek perspectives that may be missing, and plan to tell contributors how their input influenced the result.
example.reason: Input can improve the decision when there is a real opportunity to act on it. Later evaluation is useful but serves a different purpose.

source.title: Use evidence to improve access
source.deliverable: Set a practical aim and choose a process, experience and outcome measure

sections.title: Decide what improvement means
paragraphs: You have a proposed change and a clearer picture of who needs to be involved. Now ask how you will know whether it helps. Standards nine, ten and eleven connect goals, accountability, ongoing assessment and reliable demographic information to improvement.

Begin with a specific aim. For the service-planning notice, an aim might be to make the next step and assistance options easier to understand. That is more useful than a general promise to improve communication, because it points toward something you can examine.

The aim should fit your role and the available evidence. You may be preparing a recommendation rather than leading an evaluation. In that case, identify what information the responsible team would need. Do not collect personal information or create a new dataset just to complete this lesson.

sections.title: Look at process, experience and outcome
paragraphs: A process measure asks whether the planned action happened. Was the revised notice reviewed? Were assistance requests acknowledged and completed through the approved process? A process measure helps identify whether the change was implemented.

An experience measure asks how people encountered the service. Could they understand the next step? Was the assistance usable? Could they raise a concern? Experience information can explain a problem that a completion count alone does not reveal.

An outcome measure asks whether the intended result improved. Did people have a better opportunity to participate in the service-planning conversation? Choose an outcome that is meaningful and reasonably connected to the work. A high response rate does not automatically show that people understood their choices or felt respected.

You may also need a balancing question: did the change create a new burden or barrier elsewhere? A shorter notice might be easier to scan but omit information some people need. A new online option might help some people while leaving others without a usable alternative.

sections.title: Read differences carefully
paragraphs: Consider a learning example: one version of a notice receives more responses than another. That is a useful observation, but it does not prove the wording caused the difference. The timing, recipients, contact method, assistance availability or other conditions may also differ.

Ask about the denominator: how many people received each version? Ask what is missing: were undelivered notices or unanswered questions recorded? Ask whether the measure means the same thing across the groups being compared. A small count can change substantially with only a few additional responses.

Do not infer a person's language, disability, race or other identity from a name or appearance. Standard eleven concerns accurate and reliable demographic data. Any collection, use or reporting must follow applicable privacy rules, approved methods and the purpose for which the data may be used. A training exercise is not authorization to collect it.

sections.title: Protect people while learning
paragraphs: More detail is not always appropriate to publish. Small groups and combined characteristics can make individuals recognizable. Use the approved protections, reporting rules and review processes. When information is unavailable or cannot be shared safely, explain the limitation rather than inventing a conclusion.

Numbers and experience can inform each other. If a pattern suggests that a process is harder to use for some people, investigate with appropriate input from those affected and the responsible staff. Treat the difference as a prompt for inquiry, not a label attached to a community.

sections.title: Try a manageable improvement
paragraphs: A useful improvement cycle is to identify the barrier, plan an authorized change, try it at an appropriate scale, review what happened and decide what to keep or adjust. The scale depends on the work. A required official notice may need formal approval before any trial; a personal drafting practice may be easier to change.

Specify who will review the evidence and when. Without that step, a temporary fix can become permanent without anyone checking its effect. Document the reasoning so the next person can understand why the change was made.

In the activity, compare three conclusions about a changed response rate. Choose the one that acknowledges the observation, checks context and proposes an appropriate next step. Avoid both declaring success without enough evidence and dismissing the information because it is imperfect.

sections.title: Add evidence to your plan
paragraphs: For your example, write a practical aim, one process question, one experience question and one outcome question. Identify the information already available, any important limitation, the responsible role and a review date.
If your role does not include data access, do not seek it through an informal workaround. You can still ask whether an approved evaluation exists or recommend the questions that should be considered.

The next lesson addresses what happens when someone raises a concern and how to communicate progress honestly. Evidence is not only for an internal report. Used responsibly, it helps people understand what changed and what still needs attention.

practice.question: A revised notice has a higher response rate. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: The revision eliminated access barriers for everyone.
options.feedback: A response rate alone cannot establish understanding, equitable access or a single cause. That claim goes beyond the evidence.

options.text: The increase is worth examining alongside delivery, timing, group size and people's experience before deciding what it means.
options.feedback: This uses the observation while checking its limits. Look at process, experience and outcomes, and protect personal information.

options.text: The result is useless unless it proves that wording was the only cause.
options.feedback: Imperfect information can still support improvement when its limitations are clear. Use it to guide appropriate inquiry rather than dismissing it.

practice.reflection: Set a practical aim. Add one process question, one experience question, one outcome question, an information source and a review date.

example.title: Choose more than a completion count
example.situation: The team can report that a new notice was distributed, but does not yet know whether it is easier to use.
example.response: Process: was the revised notice and assistance offer used? Experience: could people explain the next step and obtain support? Outcome: was participation more achievable? Check the available information, privacy limits and other possible influences.
example.reason: An action is evidence of implementation, not proof of its effect. Combining questions gives a more useful picture.

source.title: Respond to concerns and share progress
source.deliverable: Identify an accessible concern pathway and draft a candid progress update

sections.title: Make it possible to raise a concern
paragraphs: An accessible service also needs a usable way to say that something is not working. Standard fourteen addresses culturally and linguistically appropriate ways to identify, prevent and resolve conflicts, complaints or grievances. Standard fifteen addresses communication about progress in implementing and sustaining CLAS.

For an individual learner, the practical starting point is knowing the appropriate route and explaining it clearly. You do not need to personally investigate every concern. You do need to avoid leaving someone without a next step simply because the issue belongs to another part of the organization.

sections.title: Receive the concern respectfully
paragraphs: Imagine someone says that they could not understand the service-planning notice and missed the opportunity to ask for assistance. An unhelpful response would focus only on proving that the notice was sent. A more useful response acknowledges the concern, clarifies what the person needs now, and follows the applicable process.

Do not promise a particular outcome, a deadline you cannot control, or confidentiality beyond what the process permits. Explain what you can do, what will happen next and who is responsible. If there are immediate safety issues, legal deadlines or urgent service needs, use the relevant current procedure rather than waiting for a general improvement review.

A concern may involve a misunderstanding, a service failure, discrimination, an accessibility issue or another matter requiring a specific route. Do not relabel it simply to make it fit the process most familiar to you. Obtain the appropriate guidance and preserve the person's opportunity to use available channels.

sections.title: Check the route itself
paragraphs: Ask whether someone can find the concern process, understand it and use it in a suitable language and format. A complaint form that is available only through an inaccessible website can prevent the organization from hearing the very problems it needs to address.

Consider whether the person is told how receipt will be acknowledged, what information is needed, and how to ask about progress. Use approved records and channels. Do not place complaint details or case information in this course's reflection notes.

Staff should also know how recurring concerns inform improvement. Resolving one issue may be necessary without addressing the condition that caused it. If several people encounter the same unclear instruction, the organization may need to review the instruction as well as respond to each person.

sections.title: Communicate what has changed
paragraphs: Standard fifteen asks organizations to communicate progress. Useful communication is understandable, accessible and honest about limitations. It explains what was done, what was learned and what will happen next.

For our notice, a progress update might explain that the wording and assistance information were revised after review, describe how usability is being checked, and identify the next review point. It should not claim that all communication barriers have been eliminated because one document changed.

Separate an action from a result. Updating a notice is an action. Evidence that people can use it more effectively is a result that requires checking. Keeping that distinction visible helps avoid overstating success.

sections.title: Protect privacy and preserve trust
paragraphs: Share only information approved for the audience and purpose. Avoid details that could identify a person who raised a concern. Follow the appropriate review process for public communication or organizational statements. This lesson does not authorize a learner to publish on behalf of the division.

If the evidence is incomplete, say what is known and what remains uncertain. If a change did not help as expected, explain the next step rather than hiding the result. Clear limits are more useful than a broad assurance that everything is resolved.

sections.title: Practice the response
paragraphs: In the activity, select a response to an access concern. Look for acknowledgment, a usable next step and an honest description of responsibility. Avoid an answer that dismisses the person, makes an unsupported promise or sends them elsewhere without explaining the route.

Then draft a short progress statement for your own work example. Include the issue being addressed, the action taken or proposed, how its effect will be checked and the next review point. Keep the statement general and suitable for a learning exercise.

sections.title: Prepare to bring the work together
paragraphs: You now have the main elements of a practical improvement: an understanding of the person's task, a barrier to investigate, an appropriate response, the roles needed to carry it out, input from people affected, evidence and a way to respond and report back.

The final lesson will help you assemble those elements into one usable plan. It is not a test of memorizing all fifteen numbers. It is a chance to show how the standards support a thoughtful decision and a concrete next step in your work.

practice.question: Someone says the notice was difficult to understand and they could not request assistance. Which response is most useful?

options.text: Explain that the notice was sent correctly and close the matter.
options.feedback: Sending information does not establish that it was usable. Acknowledge the concern and follow the appropriate response process.

options.text: Promise that the concern will be resolved tomorrow and kept completely confidential.
options.feedback: Do not promise an outcome, timing or confidentiality beyond your authority and the process's limits.

options.text: Acknowledge the concern, clarify the immediate need and explain the appropriate next step and responsible route.
options.feedback: This supports a usable response without making unsupported promises. Urgent needs or specific complaints may require a particular procedure.

practice.reflection: Identify the appropriate concern route. Draft a general progress statement: issue, action, evidence or limitation, and next review point.

example.title: Describe progress without overstating it
example.situation: A draft update says, 'The new notice has solved communication barriers.' Only the revision and distribution have been confirmed.
example.response: A more accurate update says that the notice and assistance information were revised, explains what review informed the change, and describes how usability will be checked at the next review point.
example.reason: Clear communication distinguishes completed actions from results still being evaluated, while protecting personal information.

source.title: Bring it together in your work
source.deliverable: Complete an improvement plan and a voluntary thirty-day review

sections.title: Return to the person and the task
paragraphs: At the beginning, you chose a work example and described what someone needs to do with it. Return to those notes. Has your understanding changed? You may now see a communication need, an unclear responsibility, a missing perspective or a way to check the result that was not obvious at first.

That is the purpose of this curriculum. The standards provide a connected way to think about service quality and access. Your plan turns that understanding into a manageable contribution within your responsibilities.
You do not need to submit private information or share your reflection to complete the learning. Use the sample notice if your own work example is too sensitive or not ready for review.

sections.title: Put the improvement into words
paragraphs: Describe the issue using an observation rather than an assumption. For our notice, some people have not responded, and the explanation of the next step and assistance options needs review. We have not concluded that people are uninterested or that wording is the only cause.

Describe the intended experience. The person should be able to understand the purpose, consider their choices, request appropriate assistance and use a clear response route. Then identify the proposed change and how it connects to the relevant standards.

The notice may connect to standard one and standard eight. Assistance arrangements connect to standards five through seven. Ownership, resources and preparation connect to standards two through four, plus standard nine. Input and evidence connect to standards ten through thirteen. Concerns and progress connect to standards fourteen and fifteen. Not every standard fits every action. Consider the wider conditions that support your plan.

sections.title: Make the plan workable
paragraphs: Identify the action you can take, the role responsible for approval or coordination, and any resources needed. Include a review point. A plan that says someone should improve communication is difficult to act on. A plan that identifies a document, a proposed revision, the person responsible and the next step is more useful.

Record what remains uncertain. Perhaps you do not know whether an assistance route is consistently available. Perhaps the right group has not yet reviewed the draft. Naming an uncertainty helps direct the next inquiry; it is not a reason to pretend the issue is resolved.

Check whether the plan creates a new barrier. If you add an online route, consider people who need another method. If you shorten a notice, check that necessary information remains. If you ask for input, ensure the process is accessible and the decision is still open enough for that input to matter.

sections.title: Test your reasoning
paragraphs: The final activity presents a proposed response to the sample notice. Review it against the whole process. Does it begin with inquiry? Does it preserve the person's choices? Does it provide a usable assistance route? Is the change within the appropriate authority? Are people affected involved? Is there a credible way to check the result?
Use the feedback to revise your reasoning. A strong answer can acknowledge uncertainty and still identify a concrete next step. It does not need to claim that one action will solve every barrier.
The goal is transfer to work. You are practicing how to recognize a situation in which these questions matter, not simply repeating a definition from a video.

sections.title: Plan a voluntary follow-up
paragraphs: Choose a reasonable time to revisit the plan, such as about thirty days after the action begins. Ask what you tried, what changed, what evidence you have and what remains to be done. If the action has not started, identify the reason and the next realistic step.

Your follow-up can be individual. If consultation would help and fits your role, you can discuss a non-sensitive summary with an appropriate colleague or supervisor. Group participation is not a requirement of this curriculum.

Distinguish completion from effect. Sending a revised document for approval is progress. Approval is another step. Evidence that people can use the information is a further question. Recognizing each stage helps you describe progress accurately.

sections.title: Reflect and choose your next step
paragraphs: Consider three optional questions. What do you understand more clearly now? What matters most for the people affected by your work? What will you do next? You can answer privately or simply think through them.

The companion sheet brings your notes together: purpose, observed barrier, relevant standards, proposed change, authority, participation, assistance, evidence, concern route and follow-up. Download it only if you want a personal working copy. Keep it in an appropriate location and do not use it as a substitute for an official case record or required approval process.

sections.title: Continue using the framework
paragraphs: You can return to any lesson or the original standards when a new situation arises. Current policy, specialist guidance and the experience of people affected remain important. The curriculum supports your judgment; it does not replace the requirements or expertise needed for a specific decision.

Thank you for taking time to examine your work carefully. Your next step does not have to be large to be useful. A clearer question, a more usable instruction, an appropriate escalation or a well-supported improvement can make participation more possible. Choose the next step you can responsibly take, and make room to learn from what happens.

practice.question: Which plan best brings the curriculum into practice?

options.text: Revise an approved process immediately, then report that access is improved.
options.feedback: The plan skips authority, participation and evidence. Distinguish the proposed action from a verified result.

options.text: Choose a specific barrier, involve the appropriate people, follow the required review, try the authorized change and revisit its effect.
options.feedback: This connects the person's experience with responsibility, participation and improvement. Keep uncertainties visible and choose a realistic next step.

options.text: Wait until every organizational barrier can be solved before taking any action.
options.feedback: A manageable authorized contribution can be worthwhile. Identify what you can responsibly do and what needs wider coordination.

practice.reflection: Bring your notes together. What is your next responsible action, and when will you revisit whether it helped?
practice.artifact: Personal improvement plan and voluntary follow-up

example.title: A complete next-step plan
example.situation: Your notes identify unclear instructions and an assistance route that needs confirmation.
example.response: Propose the revision through the person responsible; confirm the assistance process; obtain appropriate input before approval; use the authorized version; review experience and results; revisit unresolved issues at a chosen follow-up date.
example.reason: The plan links communication, responsibility, participation and evidence. It remains manageable without pretending that one notice resolves every organizational barrier.
